title: 6.2 · Made for everyone (Accessibility, usability, bias)
name: Made for everyone (Accessibility, usability, bias)
summary: Pairs audit a game they already beat with four real settings (captions, text size, contrast, left-handed), then play Design Lab in Inside the Machine: three briefs for players who see little, use one hand, or are very young. Pairs swap audit sheets and add one idea from the other pair.
iCan: find ways a game could work better for people who see, hear, read or move differently
ask another pair for an idea and add it to my own
materials: Accessibility Audit sheet printable (one per pair, picture icons)
persona cards and a paper remote (for the twin)
a chime for the sheet swap
doNow: If your partner agrees, close your eyes for ten seconds while your partner plays any game with the sound off. Write what you missed.
plan: Explore: the Settings panel on the projector
Play: audit sheet (4 minutes), then Design Lab; sheet swap at the chime

warmup.why: the unit opener (6.1 had no warm-up), one retrieval item from 6.1, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 6.1

do: Open any game on the projector and open its Settings panel (the gear). Read the switches out loud: motion, captions, read-aloud, text size, speed, assist, contrast, color cues, left-handed, graphics.
Turn captions on and text size up. Then open Inside the Machine at Design Lab (Open game at this chapter) and read brief 1 with the class.
say: Every switch here was made for someone. Captions were made for people who cannot hear, and they also help anyone on a noisy bus.
Designing for people at the edges makes things better for everyone.
ask: Who is each switch for? Who else does it help?
explore.afterAsk: Take one answer per switch, fast. Write two columns on the board, made for and also helps, and leave them up during Play.
explore.bigIdea: Designing for people at the edges makes things better for everyone.

play.goal: the audit sheet with 4 settings, then briefs 1 and 2
play.stretch: brief 3, then 3 stars, then audit a second game

steps: Pairs open Robo Route at a level they have already beaten and try 4 settings from the audit sheet one at a time: captions, text size, contrast, left-handed.
For each setting they circle could I still play (yes, kind of, no) and write who it helps.
They write two improvements for the game at the bottom of the sheet.

play.swap: at minute 14 the chime rings: pairs swap audit sheets with the next pair, read the other pair's improvements, and add one improvement they got from the other pair before handing the sheet in
play.pairs: driver and navigator on one device; the Swap! banner shows every level; the navigator holds the audit sheet and reads the brief out loud
lookFors: a pair rates a setting could still play without turning it on: ask them to show you
an improvement that is a feature, not access (more levels, better music): ask who it helps that could not play before
play.misconception: Accessibility settings are only for people with a disability; in fact captions help anyone in a noisy room and big text helps anyone in bright sun, so a change for one person usually helps many.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Which setting surprised you by helping you?
Which improvement from the other pair did you add, and why was it one you had not thought of?
showMe: One pair shows brief 2 on the projector: the two changes they picked and who else the verdict says each change helps.

exit.sentencePrompt: Name one change that would make a game work better for someone, who it helps, and who else it helps. Then name the idea you got from the other pair.
exit.frame: ___ would help ___ and also ___. The other pair gave me the idea to ___.

rubric.line: Accessibility: a change, who it helps, who else it helps
levels: Names a change and who it helps
Names a change, who it was made for and who else it helps

rubric.line: Other perspectives: used an idea from another pair
levels: Nothing yet, or no idea named
Names the other pair's idea and added it to the sheet
Says why the other pair's idea was one they had not thought of, or how it changed their own

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: picture-icon audit sheet: each setting has an icon and a three-face scale
read-aloud on; the navigator reads the brief out loud before the driver picks changes
brief 1 pre-selects one change; the pair picks the second
stretch: audit a second game with 4 different settings
brief 3, then invent a user the game forgot and write their brief on the back of the sheet

unpluggedTwin.title: Design for Sam
materials: persona cards: a Sam who sees little, a Sam who hears little, a Sam who uses one hand, a Sam who is five
a paper remote (a drawn controller with six big buttons)
steps: Each pair gets one persona card and the paper remote. They imagine playing a favorite game and mark every button and screen that would be hard for their Sam.
They redraw the remote for their Sam: bigger buttons, a shape next to every color, a one-hand layout, a read-aloud button.
Pairs swap remotes with a pair who had a different Sam and add one change the other pair's Sam needs.
Share: which change helps more than one Sam?

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: close your eyes for ten seconds while your partner plays any game with the sound off; write what you missed.

Play Inside the Machine, chapter Design Lab, in pairs for 18 minutes: the first 4 minutes trying the settings on the audit sheet, then the briefs. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 6 1 0 0. Goal: 2 briefs. Playing signed out is fine; at the chime pairs swap audit sheets and add one idea from the other pair. No devices or no internet? Run the unplugged twin printed below (Design for Sam, 15 minutes), then talk about the two discussion questions for 5 minutes.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it with the audit sheets.

audit a second game and brief 3 after Play
10 minutes of the Unit 6 review on Brain Board

notes: The settings are real: nothing new to build for the audit; any game's gear opens the same panel.
The sheet swap is the evidence for seeking other perspectives: collect the audit sheets with the added line, and read the sentence step for it.
Shared devices: this is an even lesson, so partner B signs in; the gradebook and the Standards tab count the signed-in student.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: If your partner agrees, close your eyes for ten seconds while your partner plays any game with the sound off. Write what you missed.

Big idea: Designing for people at the edges makes things better for everyone.

We will talk about:
- Which setting surprised you by helping you?
- Which improvement from the other pair did you add?

steps.title: Warm-up (live)
steps.body: Five quick questions. Your teacher shows them on the projector or starts them live.

steps.title: Play: Design Lab
steps.body:
First 4 minutes: the audit sheet. Open a level you already beat, try 4 settings from the gear, and write who each one helps.
Then Design Lab. Goal: briefs 1 and 2. Stretch: brief 3, then 3 stars.
If the game asks for a quest code, it is 6 1 0 0.
Pairs: driver and navigator. Swap when the Swap! banner shows. When the chime rings, swap audit sheets with the next pair and add one idea from theirs to yours.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about making games work for everyone.

steps.title: In your own words
steps.body:
Name one change that would make a game work better for someone, who it helps, and who else it helps. Then name the idea you got from the other pair.
Frame: ___ would help ___ and also ___. The other pair gave me the idea to ___.
